newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - BT sees huge Asia-Pacific growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - BT sees huge Asia-Pacific growth.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc (BT) plans a huge expansion in the Asia-Pacific to quadruple its annual turnover in the region to about four billion pounds ($6.4 billion) by 2000, a senior BT official said on Tuesday.
Faced with modest growth prospects in its domestic market, BT has embarked on a series of ambitious ventures that are set to make it a global telephone giant over the next few years.

The company is merging with the second biggest U.S. telephone company, MCI Communications Corp, to form Concert Plc, and is actively looking for investments across Europe to take advantage of a wave of deregulation there.
In Asia, it has targeted a series of markets for acquisitions and joint ventures, Mike Burgess, director of strategy and joint ventures for BT-Asia Pacific, told Reuters.
He said the company expected that it and its partners would invest about four billion pounds sterling in the Asia-Pacific region over the next three to four years.
"You cannot be a global player unless you are active in Asia," Burgess said in an interview. "In 20-30 years time it will be the biggest market in the world."
"We need to position ourselves now for the explosive growth that is already happening in Asia," he said. "Compound growth in cross-border, intra-Asian telecoms is 50 percent a year."
"By 2000, we expect revenue of about four billion pounds a year from the Asia Pacific region," he said.
He said an exact geographic breakdown was extremely difficult to estimate because revenue streams were entangled and crossed national and regional barriers.
Burgess declined to give an estimate of BT's current annual Asia-Pacific revenue but analysts have put it at around one billion pounds a year.
BT's global turnover was 14.73 billion pounds in 1996.

"BT recognises that to achieve revenue of four billion pounds, something of the order of four billion in investments in the region would not be unreasonable, either directly by BT or by BT and its partners," he said.
Burgess declined to say which targets, if any, BT had so far identified for acquisition but said they would come from across Asian markets, ranging from India to China and Australia.
Most of them would probably be promising businesses with existing streams of revenue. Existing international telephone carriers would be of particular interest, he said.
He said BT expected to announce several strategic alliances in the future with other telecoms players in the Asia-Pacific.
Burgess said Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT) had been identified as one of possibly three new major partners for BT in the region.

On March 13, BT announced a partnership with NTT and two state-owned firms, Singapore Power and Singapore Technologies Telemedia, to bid for a licence to become the second full telecoms service provider in Singapore.
"Within the next 12 months, we will identify a strategic partnership for at least one other...market," Burgess said.

He said BT's venture in Singapore, which analysts say is likely to cost the four-way consortium between $500 million and $1 billion, would probably not be BT's biggest single investment in the region. He declined to give further details.
($1 = 0.630 British Pounds)
